data.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
data.summary:
Input: A 2D grid of integers representing land elevations.
Output: A list of coordinate pairs where water can flow to both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans.
Rules: Water can flow from a cell to any adjacent cell in four directions if the adjacent cell's height is less than or equal to the current cell's height.

data.generator_code:
import random

def generate(rng, n):
    m = max(1, n // 10)
    cols = max(1, n // 10)
    grid = [[rng.randint(0, 100) for _ in range(cols)] for _ in range(m)]
    return [grid]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    m = max(1, n // 10)
    cols = max(1, n // 10)
    grid = [[50 for _ in range(cols)] for _ in range(m)]
    return [grid]

data.key_insight: Instead of checking if water from each cell can reach both oceans (which would be slow), we can start BFS from the ocean borders and move 'upstream' to find all cells that can reach each ocean. The intersection of the two reachable sets gives the answer.

steps.title: Initialize dimensions and queues
steps.detail: Get the number of rows (m) and columns (n). Prepare two sets, pacific_reachable and atlantic_reachable, and initialize two queues for BFS starting from the respective borders.

steps.title: Populate initial borders
steps.detail: Add Pacific border cells (top row and left column) to the Pacific queue and set. Add Atlantic border cells (bottom row and right column) to the Atlantic queue and set.

steps.title: Run BFS for Pacific ocean
steps.detail: Perform BFS from the Pacific border. From each cell, move to unvisited neighbors if the neighbor's height is greater than or equal to the current cell's height, marking them as reachable by the Pacific.

steps.title: Run BFS for Atlantic ocean
steps.detail: Perform BFS from the Atlantic border using the same upstream condition, marking cells reachable by the Atlantic.

steps.title: Find intersection
steps.detail: Find all coordinates that are present in both pacific_reachable and atlantic_reachable sets, and return them as the result.

data.pattern_summary: Traversing or searching tree or graph data structures layer by layer, useful for finding reachable nodes or shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

pattern_options.name: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We explore grid cells level by level to find paths of connected nodes that meet specific elevation conditions.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers are used for sequential data like arrays or strings, not 2D grid connectivity.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Dynamic programming applies when subproblems overlap and have optimal substructure, but grid reachability is better framed as graph traversal.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step, which does not guarantee finding all valid global paths to both borders.

Defines the edges of the graph, showing how you can move from one node to adjacent nodes.

data.brute_force_idea: Iterate through every single cell in the 2D grid, and run a separate traversal from that cell to check if it can reach both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans.
data.brute_force_why: There are m * n cells, and for each cell, the traversal can visit up to all m * n cells in the worst case.
data.bottleneck: Running separate traversals independently for every single cell leads to overlapping work and re-visiting the same paths repeatedly.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times each cell is evaluated as a starting point.
Notice that many paths overlap when you start a search from multiple individual cells.
Consider reversing the direction of the problem to start from the destinations instead of every internal cell.

data.overview: The Pacific Atlantic Water Flow problem asks us to find coordinates where water can flow to both oceans. Instead of tracing from every cell down to the oceans, we efficiently trace 'upstream' from the ocean borders using BFS and find the intersection of reachable cells.
data.intuition: Think of water flowing downhill from the peak. Going upstream means moving from lower or equal elevation to higher elevation from the perspective of the ocean edges.

data.insight: Instead of starting a traversal from every single cell to check if it can reach both oceans, the optimized solution works backwards. It starts breadth-first searches from the ocean borders themselves, moving inward to find all cells that can flow downward to the water. By tracking reachable cells in two separate sets, we can find the intersection in one final step, removing redundant traversals.

derivation.note: Iterates through rows to initialize ocean border queues.
Iterates through columns to initialize ocean border queues.
The while loop processes each grid cell at most once per BFS.
Checks the four adjacent directions for every popped cell.
Computes the set intersection of the two reachable collections.

data.time_summary: Initializing the borders takes O(m + n) time. Each BFS visits every cell and its edges at most once, taking O(m * n) operations. Finding the intersection of the two sets also takes O(m * n) in the worst case, resulting in an overall time complexity of O(m * n).
data.space_summary: The queues and visited sets store up to m * n coordinate pairs each, leading to an overall space complexity of O(m * n).
data.takeaway: When a problem asks which nodes can reach multiple target boundaries, reverse the direction of traversal by starting searches from the boundaries inward.
mistakes: Using standard depth-first search from every cell instead of reverse breadth-first search from the borders, leading to redundant work.
Forgetting to check if neighbor elevations are greater than or equal to the current cell when moving backward from the ocean.
Modifying the input matrix to track visited states instead of using a separate set or boolean matrix.
